column3: Comes after a verb or in a time phrase: 等一会, 过一会 (after a while), 一会就好. 等一下 is just as common. 会 is the same character as in 我会说, read hui4; here it is the bound form for "a moment".
column6: Qǐng děng yīhuì, wǒ mǎshàng lái.
column7: Please wait a moment, I will be right there.
column9: Comes after a verb or in a time phrase: 等一會, 過一會 (after a while), 一會就好. 等一下 is just as common. 會 is the same character as in 我會說, read hui4; here it is the bound form for "a moment".

column3: Alone it turns up mostly in set phrases and compounds; 春天 is the everyday word, and 春假 and 春节 (Spring Festival) use it too. The character combines grass, a "swollen sprout" as its sound part, and the sun.
column6: Chūn tiān lái le, huā dōu kāi le.
column7: Spring has come and the flowers are all in bloom.
column9: Alone it turns up mostly in set phrases and compounds; 春天 is the everyday word, and 春假 and 春節 (Spring Festival) use it too. The character combines grass, a "swollen sprout" as its sound part, and the sun.

column3: The everyday word is 夏天; alone 夏 is for written phrases and compounds, and it follows 春 in the order 春夏秋冬. Some scholars read an early form as a man under the scorching sun, but this is uncertain.
column6: Xià tiān tài rè le, wǒ bù xǐhuān.
column7: Summer is too hot; I don't like it.
column9: The everyday word is 夏天; alone 夏 is for written phrases and compounds, and it follows 春 in the order 春夏秋冬. Some scholars read an early form as a man under the scorching sun, but this is uncertain.

column3: Mostly met in 秋天 and in 中秋节 (Mid-Autumn Festival), when families eat mooncakes. A common explanation is that after the grain is harvested, the fields are burned to kill locusts and their eggs.
column6: Qiū tiān lái le, tiānqì liáng le.
column7: Autumn has come and the weather has cooled.
column9: Mostly met in 秋天 and in 中秋節 (Mid-Autumn Festival), when families eat mooncakes. A common explanation is that after the grain is harvested, the fields are burned to kill locusts and their eggs.

column3: Alone it is mostly in compounds: 冬天 is the everyday word, and 冬至 is the winter solstice, a day for eating tangyuan or dumplings. It ends the order 春夏秋冬.
column4: 冬天来了，我要穿厚外套。
column5: 冬天來了，我要穿厚外套。
column6: Dōng tiān lái le, wǒ yào chuān hòu wàitào.
column7: Winter has come; I need to wear a thick coat.
column9: Alone it is mostly in compounds: 冬天 is the everyday word, and 冬至 is the winter solstice, a day for eating tangyuan or dumplings. It ends the order 春夏秋冬.

column3: Both a noun and a verb: 有计画 (have a plan), 计画去日本 (plan to go to Japan). The mainland usually writes this word 计划.
column7: What plans do you have for the summer vacation?
column9: Both a noun and a verb: 有計畫 (have a plan), 計畫去日本 (plan to go to Japan). The mainland usually writes this word 計劃.

column3: Mostly used in Southeast Asia and for Chinese taught to overseas Chinese: 学华文, 华文老师. Elsewhere people say 中文 (and for spoken Mandarin 国语 in Taiwan, 普通话 on the mainland).
column7: He is studying Chinese.
column9: Mostly used in Southeast Asia and for Chinese taught to overseas Chinese: 學華文, 華文老師. Elsewhere people say 中文 (and for spoken Mandarin 國語 in Taiwan, 普通話 on the mainland).

column3: The plain word, fine to use in a shop or school. 洗手间 is more polite; signs say 化妆室 in Taiwan and usually 卫生间 on the mainland.
column7: Excuse me, where is the restroom?
column9: The plain word, fine to use in a shop or school. 洗手間 is more polite; signs say 化妝室 in Taiwan and usually 衛生間 on the mainland.

column3: Mostly met as 窗户 or 窗子, but alone in 开窗, 关窗 and 窗外. Counted with 扇: 一扇窗. One account of the word is that it is literally "where light penetrates".
column7: Please close the window.
column9: Mostly met as 窗戶 or 窗子, but alone in 開窗, 關窗 and 窗外. Counted with 扇: 一扇窗. One account of the word is that it is literally "where light penetrates".

column3: The word for air conditioning in Taiwan: 开冷气 (turn it on). The mainland usually says 空调, 开空调.
column7: The air conditioning is on in the classroom.
column9: The word for air conditioning in Taiwan: 開冷氣 (turn it on). The mainland usually says 空調, 開空調.

column3: The machine itself, counted with 台: 一台冷气机. 机 ends many appliance words, such as 洗衣机 and 照相机. In Taiwan many people just say 冷气 for the machine too; the mainland calls the unit 空调.
column7: This air conditioner is very noisy.
column9: The machine itself, counted with 台: 一台冷氣機. 機 ends many appliance words, such as 洗衣機 and 照相機. In Taiwan many people just say 冷氣 for the machine too; the mainland calls the unit 空調.

column3: Often followed by a verb: 有空来玩 (come visit when you have time). The negative is 没空. 你有空吗？ is a friendly way to ask if someone is free. 空 is read kòng here, for free time; meaning "empty" it is read kōng.
column7: Are you free tomorrow?
column9: Often followed by a verb: 有空來玩 (come visit when you have time). The negative is 沒空. 你有空嗎？ is a friendly way to ask if someone is free. 空 is read kòng here, for free time; meaning "empty" it is read kōng.

column3: Also the measure word for meals: 一天吃三餐. Mostly seen in compounds: 早餐, 午餐, 晚餐 and 餐厅 (restaurant). Its original meaning was "to swallow".
column7: He eats three meals a day.
column9: Also the measure word for meals: 一天吃三餐. Mostly seen in compounds: 早餐, 午餐, 晚餐 and 餐廳 (restaurant). Its original meaning was "to swallow".

column3: Used for games played with the feet, not only for a single kick: 踢足球, 踢球. Other ball games take other verbs; baseball and basketball use 打.
column7: He likes to play soccer.
column9: Used for games played with the feet, not only for a single kick: 踢足球, 踢球. Other ball games take other verbs; baseball and basketball use 打.

column3: The verb is 打: 打棒球; you watch it with 看棒球. On its own 棒 is also praise: 你很棒, 好棒.
column7: My older brother likes playing baseball.
column9: The verb is 打: 打棒球; you watch it with 看棒球. On its own 棒 is also praise: 你很棒, 好棒.

column3: The usual word in Taiwan, where you ride it with 骑: 骑脚踏车. The mainland says 自行车, which is also the written, formal term in Taiwan. The name is literally a foot-tread vehicle: you tread the pedals.
column7: He rides a bicycle to school every day.
column9: The usual word in Taiwan, where you ride it with 騎: 騎腳踏車. The mainland says 自行車, which is also the written, formal term in Taiwan. The name is literally a foot-tread vehicle: you tread the pedals.

column3: Taiwan says 网路 where the mainland says 网络. 上网 means to go online, and 网路很慢 means the connection is slow.
column7: The Internet here is fast.
column9: Taiwan says 網路 where the mainland says 網絡. 上網 means to go online, and 網路很慢 means the connection is slow.

column3: A verb with its object, so it can split: 聊了一个小时的天 (chatted for an hour). The person you chat with comes after 跟: 跟朋友聊天.
column7: We are chatting in the café.
column9: A verb with its object, so it can split: 聊了一個小時的天 (chatted for an hour). The person you chat with comes after 跟: 跟朋友聊天.

column3: The same word as 聊天 with the 儿 ending of northern speech; Taiwan Mandarin uses that ending much less and mostly says 聊天. It splits like a verb and its object: 聊聊天儿 (have a chat). Here 儿 is only the -r ending of northern speech, not a syllable of its own.
column7: Let's sit down and have a chat.
column9: The same word as 聊天 with the 兒 ending of northern speech; Taiwan Mandarin uses that ending much less and mostly says 聊天. It splits like a verb and its object: 聊聊天兒 (have a chat). Here 兒 is only the -r ending of northern speech, not a syllable of its own.

column3: Said when answering or making a phone call: 喂，请问哪位？ Said to a stranger face to face it sounds rude.
column7: Hello, who are you looking for?
column9: Said when answering or making a phone call: 喂，請問哪位？ Said to a stranger face to face it sounds rude.

column3: Often shortened to 机场: 去机场. 场 is a large place for one purpose, as in 操场 and 停车场, and 机 is the machine or aircraft ending of 飞机 (airplane).
column7: We take a car to the airport.
column9: Often shortened to 機場: 去機場. 場 is a large place for one purpose, as in 操場 and 停車場, and 機 is the machine or aircraft ending of 飛機 (airplane).

column3: Used for giving directions: 在十字路口左转 (turn left at the intersection), 过了十字路口. 路口 alone is also common, and 十字 is the cross in 红十字 (Red Cross).
column4: 在前面的十字路口左转。
column5: 在前面的十字路口左轉。
column7: Turn left at the intersection ahead.
column9: Used for giving directions: 在十字路口左轉 (turn left at the intersection), 過了十字路口. 路口 alone is also common, and 十字 is the cross in 紅十字 (Red Cross).

column3: A soft bag of paper or cloth, as in 纸袋; it is counted with 个. A bag with handles that you carry, such as a handbag, is usually 包.
column6: Qǐng gěi wǒ yī ge dàizi.
column7: Please give me a bag.
column9: A soft bag of paper or cloth, as in 紙袋; it is counted with 個. A bag with handles that you carry, such as a handbag, is usually 包.

column3: The full name; in speech the shorter 相机 is just as common. You take pictures with it using 照相 or 拍照, and it is counted with 台.
column6: Tā yǒu yī tái jiù de zhàoxiàngjī.
column7: He has an old camera.
column9: The full name; in speech the shorter 相機 is just as common. You take pictures with it using 照相 or 拍照, and it is counted with 台.

column3: Used only inside words, such as 头发 and 白发; on its own it is not said.
column6: Tā de tóu fà dōu bái le.
column7: His hair has all turned white.
column9: Used only inside words, such as 頭髮 and 白髮; on its own it is not said.

column3: The fuller, spoken form; 手指 is the plainer word for a finger. A single finger is counted with 根: 一根手指头. The 头 here is a noun suffix with a neutral tone; on its own 头 is tóu, the head.
column7: His finger is injured.
column9: The fuller, spoken form; 手指 is the plainer word for a finger. A single finger is counted with 根: 一根手指頭. The 頭 here is a noun suffix with a neutral tone; on its own 頭 is tóu, the head.

column3: A spoken word for a finger or a toe: 手指头 is a finger, 脚趾头 a toe. It is counted with 根, and 手指 is the plainer word for a finger.
column7: Don't point your finger at people.
column9: A spoken word for a finger or a toe: 手指頭 is a finger, 腳趾頭 a toe. It is counted with 根, and 手指 is the plainer word for a finger.

column3: Nearly always heard as 肚子: 肚子饿 for hungry, 肚子痛 for a stomachache, 拉肚子 for diarrhea. It covers the whole belly, not only the stomach 胃.
column6: Wǒ de dù zi hěn è.
column7: My stomach is hungry.
column9: Nearly always heard as 肚子: 肚子餓 for hungry, 肚子痛 for a stomachache, 拉肚子 for diarrhea. It covers the whole belly, not only the stomach 胃.

column3: The full name, fine in writing and on signs; in speech 超市 is shorter and much more common. 超级 before a noun means super-, as in 超级英雄.
column6: Wǒ cháng qù chāojíshìchǎng mǎi cài.
column7: I often go to the supermarket to buy groceries.
column9: The full name, fine in writing and on signs; in speech 超市 is shorter and much more common. 超級 before a noun means super-, as in 超級英雄.

column3: Mostly met inside words: 袜子 is the everyday word, counted by the pair with 双, and 短袜 and 长袜 are short and long socks.
column6: Wǒ mǎi le yī shuāng wà zi.
column7: I bought a pair of socks.
column9: Mostly met inside words: 襪子 is the everyday word, counted by the pair with 雙, and 短襪 and 長襪 are short and long socks.

column3: It stays inside words: 裙子 is the everyday word, and the ending names kinds, as in 短裙 and 连衣裙 (a one-piece dress). The verb is 穿: 穿裙子.
column6: Tā chuān le yī tiáo hóng qún zi.
column7: She wore a red skirt.
column9: It stays inside words: 裙子 is the everyday word, and the ending names kinds, as in 短裙 and 連衣裙 (a one-piece dress). The verb is 穿: 穿裙子.

column3: Usually 裤子, counted with 条: 一条裤子. As an ending it names kinds, as in 牛仔裤 for jeans and 短裤 for shorts.
column6: Zhè tiáo kù zi tài cháng le.
column7: These pants are too long.
column9: Usually 褲子, counted with 條: 一條褲子. As an ending it names kinds, as in 牛仔褲 for jeans and 短褲 for shorts.

column3: Usually 帽子, counted with 顶 and put on with 戴: 戴帽子. As an ending it names kinds, as in 安全帽 for a helmet. It was originally written 冃, and 目 and 巾 were added later.
column6: Tā dài zhe yī dǐng mào zi.
column7: He is wearing a hat.
column9: Usually 帽子, counted with 頂 and put on with 戴: 戴帽子. As an ending it names kinds, as in 安全帽 for a helmet. It was originally written 冃, and 目 and 巾 were added later.

column3: A variant of 其他, which is the more common spelling; 其它 is used for things, while 其他 can also mean other people. It comes before a noun, with or without 的.
column6: Qítā de dōngxi wǒ dōu bù yào.
column7: I don't want any of the other things.
column9: A variant of 其他, which is the more common spelling; 其它 is used for things, while 其他 can also mean other people. It comes before a noun, with or without 的.

column3: The characters only imitate the English sound and mean nothing together. It is counted with 个 or 份, and the filling comes before it, as in 火腿三明治.
column4: 我早上吃了一个三明治。
column5: 我早上吃了一個三明治。
column6: Wǒ zǎoshang chī le yī ge sānmíngzhì.
column7: I ate a sandwich this morning.
column9: The characters only imitate the English sound and mean nothing together. It is counted with 個 or 份, and the filling comes before it, as in 火腿三明治.

column3: A burger place is a 汉堡店. The longer 汉堡包 is also heard, mostly on the mainland.
column7: I want to eat a hamburger at noon.
column9: A burger place is a 漢堡店. The longer 漢堡包 is also heard, mostly on the mainland.

column3: In everyday speech it is mostly small cakes and sweets eaten between meals, as in 吃点心. The dim sum of a Cantonese teahouse is 点心 too.
column4: 下午我们吃了一些点心。
column5: 下午我們吃了一些點心。
column6: Xiàwǔ wǒmen chī le yīxiē diǎnxin.
column7: We ate some snacks this afternoon.
column9: In everyday speech it is mostly small cakes and sweets eaten between meals, as in 吃點心. The dim sum of a Cantonese teahouse is 點心 too.

column3: Counted by the scoop with 球 and by the cone with 支: 一球冰淇淋. On the mainland 冰激凌 is a common alternative. The last two characters are a loanword for "cream".
column7: I often eat ice cream in summer.
column9: Counted by the scoop with 球 and by the cone with 支: 一球冰淇淋. On the mainland 冰激凌 is a common alternative. The last two characters are a loanword for "cream".

column3: Leafy greens, and what a menu means by "vegetables": 炒青菜. It is what children are told to eat: 要多吃青菜. 烫青菜 (blanched greens) is a Taiwan dish name. One old explanation of 青 is "the color of growing plants", hence green or blue-green.
column7: Children should eat more green vegetables.
column9: Leafy greens, and what a menu means by "vegetables": 炒青菜. It is what children are told to eat: 要多吃青菜. 燙青菜 (blanched greens) is a Taiwan dish name. One old explanation of 青 is "the color of growing plants", hence green or blue-green.

column3: A general word for a knife, counted with 把: 一把刀子. For a dining table knife say 餐刀, and for a fruit knife 水果刀.
column6: Qǐng gěi wǒ yī bǎ dāozi.
column7: Please give me a knife.
column9: A general word for a knife, counted with 把: 一把刀子. For a dining table knife say 餐刀, and for a fruit knife 水果刀.

column3: In Taiwan the everyday word for any spoon, counted with 支: 一支汤匙. The mainland usually says 勺子. 匙 is read chí here, but shi in 钥匙, a key.
column6: Qǐng gěi wǒ yī zhī tāngchí.
column7: Please give me a spoon.
column9: In Taiwan the everyday word for any spoon, counted with 支: 一支湯匙. The mainland usually says 勺子. 匙 is read chí here, but shi in 鑰匙, a key.

column3: Cooking with dry heat, in an oven or over a fire: 烤面包 for toasting bread, 烤鸡 for roast chicken, 烤肉 for a barbecue.
column6: Wǒ xiǎng kǎo yī ge dàngāo.
column7: I want to bake a cake.
column9: Cooking with dry heat, in an oven or over a fire: 烤麵包 for toasting bread, 烤雞 for roast chicken, 烤肉 for a barbecue.

column3: Friendly and informal, so keep it out of formal writing. It shows news or feeling: 我到啦, 好啦 for "okay, okay", 来啦 for "I'm coming". It can also follow each item in a list: 苹果啦、香蕉啦.
column7: I'm here!
column9: Friendly and informal, so keep it out of formal writing. It shows news or feeling: 我到啦, 好啦 for "okay, okay", 來啦 for "I'm coming". It can also follow each item in a list: 蘋果啦、香蕉啦.

column3: After a verb it makes a request lighter: 看一下, 等一下, 帮我一下. For "suddenly" the form 一下子 is more usual.
column7: Please take a look.
column9: After a verb it makes a request lighter: 看一下, 等一下, 幫我一下. For "suddenly" the form 一下子 is more usual.
